title: Like Decimal Maker
context: Grade 5, the pages on like and unlike decimals. An adult sees a rule about adding zeros. What the pages are doing is counting the places after the point, and writing zeros at the end, after the point, so decimals line up without changing value. A whole number gets its point first. Making decimals like is a help for comparing and adding, not a rule.

writeup.why: Tell like decimals from unlike decimals by counting decimal places, and change unlike decimals, whole numbers included, into like decimals by writing zeros after the point.
writeup.look: Decimal cards with their points in one line, Like and Unlike trays under them, a tray of violet zero chips at the right, and a hundred grid under a card on the third phase.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Like Decimal Maker' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x sixty-four, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many decimal places the longest card has, so the child sees the target for the others. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x sixty-four, y 202. The cards stand one under another from y 240 in the left half of the working area, each 420 wide and 70 tall, their large near-black points all on one vertical line at x 330, the digits deep blue. The count of places sits at the right end of each card in amber once Count places is tapped. The Like decimals and Unlike decimals trays stand side by side along y 600, each 400 by 110 and labelled in ink. The tray of violet zero chips, each labelled Added zero, runs down the right of the working area at x 1000. On the third phase a hundred grid, or a strip in tenths, 300 across, sits under the card being changed at x 560, y 380, and keeps its shading as the zeros are added. On the fourth the Point first button sits at x 560, y 250, and a point it writes is violet. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across with a point key, for setting a decimal with up to three places or a whole number, or for typing a like decimal into the answer slot. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the tools of this chapter share them. A decimal or fraction the question gives is deep blue, with the shaded parts that show it. The result the working reaches, a decimal, a fraction, a sum, a difference or what is left, is green, with its shaded parts. Ten of one place traded for one of the next, a carry in adding or a trade in taking away, is vermilion. A zero written after the point to line decimals up is violet, and so is the point written after a whole number before those zeros. The part taken away, used or poured out is rose. The digit, place or step being worked on now, and the first place where two decimals differ, are amber. A zero holding a place open inside a number is grey, and nothing else on the stage is ever grey. An unshaded part stays warm white inside its near-black outline, the decimal point is near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey. Chrome never borrows one of them, and each of those readings survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label, Given, Answer, Carry, Trade, Added zero, Taken away, Left or Place holder, before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last set of cards made like, their points in one line and the added zeros in violet.

source_tool.description: Decimal cards stand one under another in the working area with their points in one vertical line, each decimal deep blue. A Count places button lights the digits after each point in amber and writes the count at the right of the card, and two trays under the cards, Like decimals and Unlike decimals, take a set of cards by drag. A tray of violet zero chips labelled Added zero sits at the right. A chip dropped at the end of a decimal, after the point, settles there, and a hundred grid, or a strip in tenths, under the card keeps exactly the same shading, so the value is seen not to change. On the last phase a whole number card has no point; a zero chip dropped straight onto it makes the card jump to ten times the number, the jump shown in words, and the chip slides back off. A Point first button writes a violet point after the ones digit, and then the zero chips settle after it. A number pad sets any decimal with up to three places or any whole number up to ninety-nine. The running count at the top left of the canvas says how many decimal places the longest card has.

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: strips cut into ten equal parts, hundred grids of ten rows and ten columns, place value charts with a column for each place, column sums with their points in one line, and measuring jugs, ropes and scales marked in tenths.

Every whole is drawn the same size as every other whole it is compared or combined with, and its parts are exactly equal: a strip in tenths has ten parts of one width, and a hundred grid is always a full ten by ten.
The decimal point is drawn large and always sits between the ones and the tenths. In a column, every point lies on one vertical line.
A place value chart names every column above its digit: Hundreds, Tens, Ones, the point, Tenths, Hundredths, Thousandths.
Where shaded cells are counted, exactly the stated number is shaded, and they stay countable at a glance.

Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: a strip cutting into tenths, ten tenths sliding together into one whole, a zero appearing after the point, or a carry moving to the next place.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit or a part the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a decimal plays in a piece of working: every decimal or fraction the question gives is deep blue, with the shaded parts that show it, and every result the working reaches, a decimal, a fraction, a sum or a difference, is green, with its shaded parts; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Ten of one place traded for one of the next place, a carry in adding or a trade in taking away, is vermilion. A zero written at the end, after the point, to make like decimals is violet, and so is the point written after a whole number before those zeros. The part taken away, used or poured out is rose. The digit, place or step being worked on now, and the first place where two decimals differ, are amber. A zero holding a place open inside a number is grey. An unshaded part of a whole stays warm white inside its outline, and the decimal point itself is near-black ink. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Carry, Trade, Added zero, Taken away, Left and Place holder, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.

phase_map.concept: Whole numbers get a point first

placement.where: After the class has written decimals on slips and laid zero cards after them by hand. The tool is what shows under each zero that the shaded amount did not move, and what shows a whole number jumping when a zero goes straight onto it.

answer_key.rule: The decimal places of a decimal are the digits after its point. Decimals with the same number of decimal places are like decimals, and decimals with different numbers of decimal places are unlike decimals. To make them like, write zeros at the end, after the last digit to the right of the point, until they have the same number of places; the value does not change. A whole number has its point after the ones digit: write the point first, then the zeros. Zeros are added only after the point. Making decimals like is a help, not a rule.
answer_key.wrong: The card is shown again with its places lit and counted, and the child's card is set beside it with its own hundred grid, so the child sees whether the shading moved. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Count only the digits after the point.
6.02 has 0 and 2 after the point: two places.
13.47 has two places, and 0.93 has two places.
All three have two decimal places, so they are like decimals.
items.answer: Each has two decimal places, so they are like decimals
items.question: How many decimal places do 6.02, 13.47 and 0.93 have? Are they like decimals?
items.checkpoint: Like decimals have the same number of decimal places.
items.misconception: Counting every digit, so 13.47 seems to have four places, though the 1 and 3 are before the point.

steps: 7.1 has one digit after the point: one decimal place.
7.105 has three digits after the point: three decimal places.
The numbers of places are different, so they are unlike decimals.
items.answer: No. 7.1 has one decimal place and 7.105 has three, so they are unlike decimals
items.question: Are 7.1 and 7.105 like decimals?
items.checkpoint: Unlike decimals have different numbers of decimal places.
items.misconception: Calling them like because both start with 7.1, though the number of places after the point is what decides.

steps: 5.136 has three decimal places and 2.4 has one.
Write two zeros at the end of 2.4, after the last digit to the right of the point: 2.400.
The value does not change, because 4 tenths is 400 thousandths.
Now 2.400 and 5.136 both have three decimal places.
items.question: Make 2.4 and 5.136 like decimals.
items.checkpoint: Zeros written at the end, after the point, do not change the value.
items.misconception: Writing the zeros in front of the 4, as 2.004, which puts them inside the number and makes it much smaller.

steps: 8 is a whole number, so its point sits after the ones digit.
3.25 has two decimal places, so write one more zero after the point: 8 = 8.00.
Now 8.00 and 3.25 both have two decimal places.
items.question: Make 8 and 3.25 like decimals.
items.checkpoint: Write the point first, then the zeros. Zeros are added only after the point.
items.misconception: Writing two zeros straight onto 8, which makes 800, a hundred times as big.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: How many decimal places does 14.306 have?
items.final_answer: 3, because three digits come after the point

items.question: Are 0.6 and 0.66 like or unlike decimals?
items.final_answer: Unlike. 0.6 has one decimal place and 0.66 has two

items.question: Which two of 3.14, 31.4 and 0.72 are like decimals?
items.final_answer: 3.14 and 0.72. Each has two decimal places, and 31.4 has one

items.question: Write the whole number 12 with three decimal places.
items.final_answer: 12.000. Write the point first, then three zeros after it

items.question: Do 5.20, 5.2 and 5.200 have the same value? Are they like decimals?
items.final_answer: They have the same value, because zeros at the end after the point change nothing. They are unlike decimals, with two, one and three decimal places

teaching_notes: Count decimal places by counting the digits after the point, never the digits of the whole number part. Zeros written at the end, after the point, change nothing; show it on a hundred grid, where eight tenths and eighty hundredths shade the same squares. A whole number gets its point first: a zero straight onto a whole number makes it ten times as big. Making decimals like is a help for comparing and for lining up sums, not a rule that must come first.

The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Count the digits after each point. Add zeros after the point until the counts match. A whole number gets its point first.
